title: "... students don't have misconceptions."
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Meyer takes up Rochelle Gutierrez's claim that students do not have misconceptions, only conceptions that make sense to them until they meet something that breaks them. He argues that teachers who fixate on a misconception are really fixated on what they themselves know. Citing Ausubel, he shows the critique is cognitive and pedagogical as well as social, since teaching improves when it starts from what students know. A graphing-inequalities example shows the move in practice: he affirms the students' idea, then has them test a value that exposes its limits. He closes by saying professional development in teaching doubles as personal development, because the same curiosity about others' sense-making applies at home and in the community.
points: Reframing an error as a conception treats the student's idea as sensible and bounded rather than as a defect to correct.
Ausubel's point that prior knowledge is the key factor gives the reframe a cognitive grounding, not just a social one.
In the inequality lesson, Meyer validated the students' rule and then supplied a case that exposed its limit, letting students revise it themselves.
Meyer ties the stance to personal growth, claiming that teaching work transforms the teacher as a person.
quotes: They have conceptions. And those conceptions make sense for them, until they encounter something that no longer works. They are only “misconceptions” when we begin with the expectation that others need to come to our way of thinking or viewing the world.

Over the last ten years, math education has done a top-shelf job destigmatizing making mistakes and revealing misconceptions. But when teachers fixate on the idea of a student having a misconception, even if to say that’s okay!, they are fixated on what they themselves know.

Psychologist David Ausubel said, “The most important single factor influencing learning is what a learner already knows.” So Gutierrez’s critique isn’t purely social here; it’s also cognitive and pedagogical. Our teaching is less effective when we’re focused on what we know and more effective when we focus on what students know.

These students don’t have a misconception. They have a conception, an idea, that whatever number is by itself on one side of an inequality, that’s the critical point. They need to encounter something that helps them find the limits of that idea.

Then we evaluated x = 20 and convinced ourselves that it definitely works in the graph but definitely not in the inequality where it produces the false statement 34 ≤ 25. Then I asked students to discuss what they saw at their table, try again, and people found a new path.

What I’m saying is that PD is also PD–professional development in teaching is personal development in life. This is not true for many, many jobs on offer. But because our work is social and very intensely personal, personal transformation results in professional transformation and vice versa.
